frameworks.name: Client-Financed Acquisition (CFA)
frameworks.definition: A model where 30-day gross profit from one new customer exceeds the cost of acquiring and fulfilling two customers, enabling unlimited growth with no external capital.

frameworks.name: Never Go Hungry Framework (Six Traffic Sources)
frameworks.definition: Six always-available pools for new customers: paid media, earned media, owned media, outbound, affiliates/partners, and referrals; each individually capable of generating $20M+ in revenue.

frameworks.name: Grand Slam Offer (Seven Components)
frameworks.definition: A seven-element offer construction system: promotion type (free/discount/premium), core offer, bonuses, scarcity, urgency, guarantees, and magic naming formula; designed to make offers so compelling prospects feel foolish declining.

frameworks.name: Six Levers of Lifetime Gross Profit
frameworks.definition: Six levers to maximize revenue per customer: (1) increase price, (2) reduce cost of fulfillment, (3) increase purchase frequency, (4) upsell (more or better), (5) downsell, (6) cross-sell adjacent needs.

frameworks.name: Value Equation (Four Drivers)
frameworks.definition: A four-variable formula for perceived value: (dream outcome x perceived likelihood of achievement) / (time delay x effort and sacrifice). Increasing the numerator or decreasing the denominator increases willingness to pay.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a business can grow with zero external capital if 30-day gross profit from one new customer exceeds the combined cost of acquiring and fulfilling two customers: if 30-day cash > (CAC + COGS) x 2, the business is self-financing and can compound customers by reinvesting each credit-card cycle.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business has a 30-day payment window (credit card or equivalent)
Gross profit is collected within 30 days of acquisition
Applies regardless of business model when the math condition is satisfied
claims.mechanism: Credit card float provides 30-day interest-free capital; as long as gross profit collected in that window exceeds two customers' CAC plus COGS, the business generates net positive cash flow each cycle and can reinvest without needing outside funding.
bounded_by: Breaks down when operational capacity (fulfillment, staffing) cannot scale with customer volume
Does not apply if gross profit is collected after 30 days

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that free offers convert at 5 to 10 times the rate of any other promotion type (discount or premium), making them the correct starting point for any new business or new acquisition channel before monetization is layered in.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies when launching a new offer or entering a new channel
The free offer is used to generate flow, then the paid offer is introduced as an upsell
claims.mechanism: Removing price friction eliminates the largest barrier to action; once prospects are in motion (flow), monetization via upsell is substantially easier than converting cold to paid.

numbers.axis: conversion rate relative to non-free offers

anchors.value: 5-10x conversion rate of discount or premium offers

bounded_by: Does not imply free offers maximize revenue per acquisition; they maximize volume, monetized via upsell

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that doubling price is the most powerful of the three growth levers (more customers, higher price, more purchases per customer): in a business with 20% gross margins at $100/month, a 50% price increase with costs held flat more than doubles net profit, while doubling customer count or purchase frequency only doubles it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Assumes fixed costs of fulfillment
Applies to service or subscription businesses with meaningful gross margin
claims.mechanism: Price increases flow entirely to margin because fulfillment cost is fixed; more customers or more purchases require proportional fulfillment cost, leaving margin ratio unchanged. The price lever is the only one that expands the margin percentage.

anchors.region: double purchase frequency / cut churn in half
anchors.value: 2x profit (same outcome as doubling customers, but higher LTV per customer)

anchors.region: double price (at 20% original margin, costs fixed)

bounded_by: Assumes market will absorb the price increase without proportional drop in conversion
Does not apply if fulfillment costs scale proportionally with price

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that improving the offer (rather than changing traffic source or platform) is the primary multiplier on marketing ROI: in a B2B lead generation example at $10,000/month ad spend, switching from a $1,500/month retainer model to a pay-per-appointment model raised upfront revenue from $5,000 to $112,000 on the same ad budget, representing a 2.5x lift in response rate and a 2.3x lift in close rate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B agency serving small businesses
$10,000/month ad spend held constant
Same impressions and show rate before and after
claims.mechanism: A pay-per-result pricing structure eliminates the prospect's risk of paying for no leads; this increases response rate because the offer is risk-free, and increases close rate because the sales conversation starts from a position of aligned incentives.
bounded_by: Example is specific to B2B lead generation agencies; payoff structure differs by business model

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the business owner who can generate more lifetime gross profit per customer than competitors wins the acquisition arms race, because higher LTGP allows outbidding competitors for every eyeball in the shared media market, creating a legal monopoly on audience attention.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Competing in paid media channels where CPM/CPC is set by auction
Multiple competitors targeting the same audience
claims.mechanism: In auction-based paid media, the highest bidder wins all impressions at their target CPM. A business with 5x higher LTGP can profitably bid 5x higher, pricing all competitors out of the audience auction and capturing 100% of impressions.
bounded_by: Applies to paid media auction channels; does not apply to organic, referral, or non-auction channels where CPM is not bid-dependent

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that branded search advertising (paying to appear when users search for your own company name) consistently delivers 20-40:1 return on ad spend and is the easiest, most-neglected high-ROI paid media tactic available to most businesses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business already has brand recognition in its market
Competing bidders are purchasing the brand's name as a keyword
claims.mechanism: Users searching for a brand by name are already in high-intent purchase mode; CPCs on branded terms are low because competitors rarely bid on exact brand names, while conversion rates are highest among all search traffic.

numbers.axis: return on ad spend for branded search vs. general paid media

anchors.region: typical paid media ROAS (Hormozi portfolio benchmark)

bounded_by: Requires an existing brand that prospects are already searching for
Returns diminish as brand awareness is low or search volume is negligible

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that outbound sales (cold email, cold calls, direct mail, DMs) reaches approximately 20:1 return on investment after a 90-day ramp period, with 100 outreach contacts per day as the minimum threshold to generate compounding results within 6 months.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Sustained minimum of 100 outreach contacts per day
Multi-channel outbound (email, phone, DM) rather than single-channel
6-month commitment with no ROI expected in months 1-2
claims.mechanism: Outbound compounds because early contacts become warm on follow-up, referrals surface from early conversations, and script quality improves with volume; the first 60 days build the pipeline that pays off in months 3-6.

anchors.value: positive ROI; scales to ~20:1 with sustained volume (Hormozi's reported current outbound ROI)

bounded_by: Hormozi allocates 10-20% of total ad spend budget to outbound as a separate channel
Results depend heavily on niche; learning curve is niche-specific and not transferable from other industries

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that integrating a partner's product into the fulfillment onboarding process of an existing customer base (rather than running standalone affiliate promotions) produces the highest volume per founder-hour of any acquisition channel at scale.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Partner has an existing customer base with a relevant activation or onboarding problem
Your product solves a known friction point in the partner's customer journey
Integration is placed inside partner's onboarding flow, not as an external promotion
claims.mechanism: Onboarding integration captures the customer at highest-intent moment (just purchased), eliminates competition from competing offers, and leverages the partner's trust capital; the partner is incentivized because the integration solves their churn or activation problem.
bounded_by: Requires identifying a partner whose customers have the exact activation problem your product solves
Weaker when the partner relationship is purely commission-based without a genuine product problem being solved

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the optimal referral program goal is for the percentage of customers who refer to exceed the percentage of customers who churn each period; achieving this creates a self-sustaining customer base that grows with no additional acquisition spend.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business tracks referral rate and churn rate separately by cohort
Referral incentives are integrated into the onboarding process at the activation point
claims.mechanism: If referral rate > churn rate, each departing customer is replaced by more than one new customer, creating geometric growth without acquisition cost; this is the customer-success analog to client-financed acquisition.
bounded_by: Requires active referral program infrastructure embedded in onboarding; does not happen organically in most businesses

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the optimal moment to request a referral or testimonial is immediately after the customer's first activation point (the first positive result), because at that moment the customer's positive affect toward the business is at its peak; waiting even weeks materially reduces referral yield due to asymmetric memory decay between giver and receiver of value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business has an identifiable activation point (first result, first magical moment)
Referral or testimonial ask is structured into the onboarding sequence
claims.mechanism: Immediately after a positive experience, the customer's emotional state is maximally favorable and the favor feels recent and large to the recipient; over time, the doer (business) feels it did more, while the recipient (customer) remembers less, creating a window that narrows quickly.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that prepaid bundles (e.g., buy three months get one free) produce one-fifth the churn rate of month-to-month subscriptions because upfront commitment functions as a psychological lock-in mechanism.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service or subscription business with recurring delivery
Prepaid option is offered at comparable or slightly elevated total cost to monthly
claims.mechanism: Sunk cost and commitment consistency reduce the probability of cancellation; customers who have paid upfront rationalize continued engagement to justify the spend.

numbers.axis: churn rate relative to payment structure

bounded_by: Hormozi does not specify the business type or cohort size behind the 1/5 figure; treat as directional

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that upsell offers should be priced at approximately 5 times the core offer to double revenue from an existing customer base, because the Pareto principle predicts that roughly 1 in 5 customers will accept any given upsell regardless of price multiple, making a 5x upsell the mathematically efficient lever to double total revenue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business already has a defined core offer
Upsell addresses a clearly differentiated higher tier (quality, speed, or access)
Applies to service and information businesses with scalable delivery
claims.mechanism: Pareto fractal: 20% of customers will buy the next tier at any reasonable price multiple; a 5x price means 1 of 5 buyers doubles the per-customer revenue, which doubles total revenue at similar or higher margins if fulfillment cost increment is low.

numbers.axis: revenue impact of upsell tier by price multiple and take rate

anchors.value: doubles total revenue from existing base

bounded_by: Assumes upsell is a meaningfully different offer, not a trivially incremental add-on
Pareto take-rate assumption is directional; actual take rates depend on offer differentiation and sales execution

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that downsell offers (a lesser version of the core offering presented after a no) should carry higher percentage margins than the core offer, because reduced scope or service level eliminates high-cost fulfillment components while preserving most of the customer's perceived value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Core offer includes high-cost features (e.g., one-on-one access, guarantees, live support)
Downsell removes one or more of those features
Sales rep is trained and incentivized to offer the downsell after a hard no
claims.mechanism: Removing high-variable-cost features (live support, personalization, guarantees) dramatically lowers fulfillment cost while keeping list price close to core; the result is a margin-accretive version of a sale that would otherwise be lost.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the core offer has no high-cost distinguishing features to remove

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that cross-selling adjacent products (the customer's next natural need before or after purchase) is the highest-margin revenue expansion lever, and that businesses can be entirely structured around a below-cost core offer subsidized by cross-sell gross profit, as in the McDonald's model where core product earns $0.18 gross and cross-sell (fries + drink) earns $1.14.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business has identified the natural adjacent needs of its customer immediately before and after purchase
Cross-sell product can be sourced or referred at 30-50% margin or better
claims.mechanism: Customers who have just made a purchase decision are in a high-compliance state; introducing the adjacent product at that moment captures demand that exists anyway but is typically fulfilled elsewhere, with zero additional acquisition cost.

numbers.axis: gross profit per transaction component at McDonald's (Digital Marketer example cited by Hormozi)

anchors.value: $1.14 gross profit; ~6x the core product margin

bounded_by: Requires genuinely adjacent needs, not arbitrary product additions
Loss-leader core offer strategy requires sufficient cross-sell take rate to be net positive

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a quarterly four-day promotional blitz (heavy push with real scarcity on a named offer) is the most neglected high-yield tactic for monetizing owned email, SMS, and messenger lists, because lists are typically underworked between launches.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business has an owned list (email, SMS, messenger) with existing subscribers
Four-day blitz uses genuine scarcity tied to a named, time-limited promotion
Implemented at most once per quarter per list segment
claims.mechanism: Owned media has near-zero marginal reach cost; intermittent high-intensity promotion extracts revenue from subscribers who are warm but not self-initiating, without burning the list through chronic over-promotion.
bounded_by: Requires a real reason-why or named promotion to avoid appearing spammy
Over-frequency (more than quarterly) increases unsubscribe rates

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that in his companies, implementing any single neglected acquisition tactic from his six traffic source checklist produced at minimum a 20-40% increase in new customer count.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business had not previously deployed the specific tactic
Tactic selected was the highest-opportunity gap in the business's acquisition mix

numbers.axis: new customer count lift from implementing one neglected traffic source tactic

bounded_by: Hormozi does not disclose cohort size or specific company types behind this figure
Lift is from the first implementation; subsequent tactics produce diminishing incremental gains

examples.text: Alex Hormozi opened Gym Launch after losing everything when his co-founder was indicted for fraud. Starting from a near-zero bank account, he applied client-financed acquisition: spending on ads, collecting upfront fees plus supplement sales within 30 days, and reinvesting each cycle. Gym Launch went from $0 to $2.4 million per month in 18 months running 74% net margins. Prestige Labs (supplements) went from $0 to $1.7 million per month in 6 months. An Allen (agency software) investment went from $40,000 to $700,000 per month in 10 months. All were grown without external capital by ensuring the 30-day cash math was positive from day one.

When Alex Hormozi ran gyms, he struggled to sell a $99/month boot camp and could not close people on free trials. He switched to a free six-week challenge: members paid $600 upfront with a 20-pound money-back guarantee, then received a $300 supplement upsell 48 hours after joining, and were offered a membership close 21 days in (with the $600 applied as credit) that converted at 70-80%. The cash sequence was $600 deposit plus $300 supplements in the first 30 days, then 12-month EFT recurring revenue. This allowed him to sign a gym lease, staff fully, and have all payroll covered before the first EFT payment arrived, enabling him to open 6 gyms in 3 years starting at age 23 with no outside capital.

Prestige Labs (Hormozi's supplement company) achieved greater revenue than his gym business by integrating supplement sales into the onboarding of every gym Gym Launch worked with. When a new gym member joined, 48 hours later a nutrition consultation was conducted and supplements were sold. All of the partner gyms' acquisition spend funneled supplement sales to Prestige Labs at zero additional marketing cost. The model ultimately scaled to 4,000 brick-and-mortar affiliate locations. This is the concrete example Hormozi uses to illustrate full B2B partner channel integration (not just webinars or one-off promotions).

In a consulting engagement with a B2B agency spending $10,000/month on ads, Hormozi restructured the offer from $1,000 down plus $1,500/month retainer to a $4,000 flat fee with a pay-per-appointment model (no charge until a prospect showed up). On the same impression volume, response rate increased 2.5x, booking rate increased, close rate increased 2.3x, and price quadrupled. Upfront revenue on $10,000 ad spend went from $5,000 to $112,000. The agency was generating 11.2:1 returns before any recurring back-end revenue was counted.

A Hormozi consulting client serving physical therapists wanted to build a B2B partner channel. Hormozi suggested reaching out to orthotics, brace, and recovery band manufacturers who distribute through PT clinics and offering to train the manufacturer's PT clients how to sell those products better, in exchange for the manufacturer sending its PT client list. The PT business would solve the manufacturer's sales training problem, capture the PT clinics as its own clients, and be able to sell its own services on the same visit. This illustrates the principle that teaching a partner to sell their own product better is the most effective lever for unlocking partner distribution.

practices.text: Run $100/day Facebook lead ads as the starting point for any paid media program: Google how to run a Facebook lead ad, connect it to Google Sheets via Zapier, give away something free targeted at your customer list (or a lookalike audience), and collect phone numbers. This setup takes under 60 minutes and replicates what third-party lead gen companies charge five times more to deliver.

Own your branded search terms in Google Ads immediately: target every variation of your company name as paid keywords, send traffic to a simple email/phone opt-in page, and capture the highest-intent traffic in your market at a fraction of general keyword CPCs.

Send a nine-word email to your list periodically: 'Do you still need help with [problem]?' with no other content. Guaranteed to generate replies from subscribers who have a current need but have not self-initiated.

Stack two guarantees on any offer: an unconditional short-term satisfaction guarantee (love it or leave it) plus a conditional results guarantee tied to specific activation behaviors (attendance, payment, defined actions). Present the conditional guarantee as a near-certain outcome if the prospect meets the conditions.

Reskin the same offer with a new name every promotional cycle to maintain urgency and scarcity without changing operations: use the MAGIC naming formula (Magnetic reason why + Avatar announced + Goal + Interval or container + name).

Always present bonuses after the core offer, stacking them one at a time in response to hesitation; never pre-load bonuses before the initial ask, because bonuses lose anchoring power when they appear alongside the primary product rather than after a no.

Identify the three largest potential partner relationships in your market and invest materially to secure them (direct mail with cash, in-person visit, high-value gift); treat partner acquisition with the same budget seriousness as paid media.

Survey your longest-retained customers to identify their activation behavior (what they did in the first 30 days that predicted long tenure), then engineer that behavior into the onboarding sequence for all new customers.

Reduce cost of fulfillment by auditing semi-skilled administrative tasks that can be outsourced at $4/hour, and by replacing manual processes with software tools (auto-captioning, design tools, AI chat efficiency) before scaling headcount.
